head:
Action plans by profile · Adult living with obesity

Starting to move when your weight is high

If you live with a high body weight, you have probably already heard a thousand pieces of advice, many of them centred on the scales. This article starts from somewhere else: what movement does for you even if your weight barely changes, what it does for weight, and how to start without getting injured, in steps, by measuring your fitness rather than your weight. This is not a personal programme, it is a typical pathway, with what is established and what is a proposal.

The question

Let us take a typical character, illustrative, who corresponds to no one: a 44-year-old adult, at a desk all day, a BMI around 36, several diets behind him, a knee that protests on the stairs, short of breath as soon as he hurries. He has already tried to “get started”. Each time the goal was a number on the scales, and when the number did not follow, everything stopped.

If movement barely changes weight, what is it for? And where do you start when everything is heavier, more breathless, sometimes more painful, and when some gyms may have made you feel unwelcome?

The question

What can physical activity do for you independently of weight loss, what can you ask of it for weight itself, and how do you start without injuring or exhausting yourself, when your starting point is a high body weight?

This article is for adults. For children and teenagers, the rules, the doses and the role of parents are different: they are covered in the articles “My child is out of shape: where to start?” and “The teen who no longer moves: where to restart, and how to keep going” in this series, which you should turn to.

What is at stake

Your health. If weight is the only measure of success, you miss what activity does anyway: blood pressure, blood glucose, sleep, capacity for effort. These gains often arrive before the scales move, or without them.

Your method. A weight goal depends on many things outside your control. A walking or strength test can be repeated and compared with yourself.

Your independence and your dignity. Climbing a flight of stairs, carrying the shopping, getting up from a chair are abilities that can be trained. A high body weight is not a character flaw: this article does not judge you and does not give you any diet.
rest:
What the research says for this profile

The demonstration goes from the most general to the most concrete: does fitness matter at every weight? What does movement do without the scales? What does it do for weight? What happens to muscle, particularly under medical treatment? And what remains uncertain?

Step 1 of 5

At every weight, fitness is linked to the health trajectory

Cardiorespiratory fitness (the ability of your heart, lungs and muscles to sustain effort) is studied enough that an American Heart Association statement (Ross and colleagues, 2016) makes it a “clinical vital sign”. In the copy read: a meta-analysis of 33 studies and about 103,000 people finds 70% more mortality in the least fit than in the fittest third; each MET gained (a unit of capacity for effort) is associated with 15% less mortality; and fitness predicts outcomes whatever the weight. The at-risk threshold is placed below 5 METs.1,2 A meta-analysis in the British Journal of Sports Medicine (2025, 20 cohorts, 398,716 observations) crosses fitness and weight:

People with low fitness have about twice the risk, whatever their weight

Risk ratio of all-cause death (95% interval) compared with the “normal weight, fit” group. 20 cohorts, 398,716 observations. Source: meta-analysis, British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2025.3

What this means

A ratio of 1 means the same risk as the reference. Fit people, whether overweight (0.96) or living with obesity (1.11), cannot be detectably distinguished from the reference; unfit people are around 1.8 to 2.0, lean or not. For weight, this means that fitness is a legitimate target in its own right. Caution: the interval for fit obesity (0.88 to 1.40) does not rule out a small excess of risk.

Barry and colleagues (2014) had already found that at any BMI, unfit people had about double the risk.4,5 The full demonstration, objections included, is in the article “Being thin is not being fit” in the series. These are associations observed in large populations, not proof that gaining fitness changes your risk: the next step looks at effects measured in trials.

Step 2 of 5

Movement acts on your body even when the scales do not move

The 2026 AHA statement on physical activity and obesity brings together effects that are independent of weight loss. In adults with overweight or obesity (54 trials), exercise lowers systolic pressure by 3.0 mmHg and diastolic by 1.9; insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) falls by 0.34, and by 0.50 with type 2 diabetes.8 The 2006 Cochrane review (43 trials, 3,476 people) found 0.2 mmol/L lower fasting blood glucose for exercise alone, and its authors conclude that exercise “is associated with an improvement in cardiovascular risk factors even if no weight is lost”.9 These effects are modest, a few mmHg, but they do not depend on your weight: your scales can stay steady for three months while your blood pressure has come down.

Another example specific to this profile, sleep apnoea:

Training reduces sleep apnoea, with little weight loss

Change in the apnoea-hypopnoea index (95% interval). In the 2014 meta-analysis, body mass index changes by 1.4 points, not significantly; in the 2024 one, it falls by 0.7. Sources: Iftikhar et al., Lung, 2014; meta-analysis of 12 trials, 2024.13,14

What this means

A drop of 6 to 7 events per hour is useful but does not replace treatment: in a network of 80 trials, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) reduces the index by 25 events per hour; exercise, however, improves daytime sleepiness.14 If you have apnoea, movement complements your treatment.

Fitness can be trained at a higher weight too: in a meta-analysis of 53 trials on high-intensity intervals, adults with overweight gained on average 3.54 mL/kg/min of VO2max (5.45 in healthy adults).15 And in 14,345 men followed for six years, it was the change in fitness, not the change in BMI, that was associated with survival (15% less mortality per MET gained); the cohort was about 90% men of normal weight or with overweight: the result does not hold as it stands for severe obesity.7 What remains is the scales themselves.

Step 3 of 5

For weight itself, exercise helps, but less than people think

Jayedi and colleagues (2024, 116 trials, 6,880 adults) put a figure on the dose: about 0.5 kg lost per 30 minutes of weekly aerobic exercise, that is 2.8 kg at 150 minutes per week and 4.2 kg at 300, with strong heterogeneity.10 The AHA (2026) sums up: exercise alone is unlikely to produce a 5% weight loss except at very high volumes (about 225 to 420 minutes per week), and fewer than 15% of participants in aerobic trials reach it.8 Swift and colleagues (2018) likewise conclude that 150 minutes improve heart health but are generally not enough to lose weight without calorie restriction.11 Washburn and colleagues (2014, 20 trials) compare the strategies at 12 months and beyond:

Exercise alone brings little weight loss; it adds a little to diet

Median weight loss at 12 months or more, in different trials for each comparison (few trials, wide ranges). Source: Washburn et al., PLoS One, 2014.12

What this means

If your goal is to lose weight, exercise is not the main tool. Added to diet it brings a little more (8.8% versus 6.9%), but the difference was significant in only 2 trials out of 5. Regain after stopping was about 55% of the loss, with no clear difference between groups. In the high-dose trial cited by the AHA, participants did on average 179 of the 300 weekly minutes prescribed: sticking with it is the real problem.8,12

Nutrition: outside this scope

Weight also depends on diet, sleep, medications and history that this article cannot examine: it offers you no diet and no calorie calculation. The Haute Autorité de santé (HAS, June 2022, read in a press report) recommends a moderate, individualised reduction in energy intake, attentive to hunger and satiety, advises against unbalanced or very restrictive diets, and considers a medication if well-conducted nutritional care gives less than 5% loss at six months.18 These are decisions for a doctor, a dietitian or an obesity team.

Movement clearly protects another part of the body, especially when weight is lost: muscle.

Step 4 of 5

Muscle matters, especially when you lose weight, and even more under medical treatment

When weight falls, part of the loss comes from lean mass, of which muscle is the main component. In Washburn, fat-free mass fell by a median of 1.7 kg with diet alone and by 0.6 kg with aerobic exercise alone; the authors note that it “tends to be preserved” with exercise, with limited evidence.12 In older adults on a diet, a meta-analysis of 6 studies cited by the AHA finds that resistance training prevented about 93% of the loss of lean mass.8

For recent treatments (GLP-1 agonists and derivatives), the AHA reports that lean mass accounted for about 45% of the weight lost with semaglutide and 25.7% with tirzepatide, depending on the trials and measurements; no trial has studied strength training specifically with these medications.8 In a Danish trial (Lundgren, 2021, 195 adults, BMI 32 to 43), after eight weeks of diet, exercise, liraglutide or both were compared for one year:

Exercise added to the medication improves fitness; the medication alone, little

Gain in cardiorespiratory fitness at one year (95% interval), randomised trial. The exercise was mainly cycling and running at vigorous intensity, supervised. Source: Lundgren et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2021, figures taken from the 2026 AHA statement.16,8

What this means

The medication alone did not improve fitness detectably (the interval contains zero); exercise did. Exercise had increased lean mass and the combination had preserved it, for a total weight loss of 15.7% versus 13.4% with the medication alone.16,17 The trial is not about strength training: the value of strength under treatment is a reasonable hypothesis, not a fact demonstrated for you. If a treatment has been prescribed to you, talk to the person who follows you.

Step 5 of 5

What remains uncertain, and the importance weight keeps

It would be dishonest to conclude that weight does not matter. In the Global BMI Mortality Collaboration analysis (239 studies, more than 10 million people), the risk of death rises with BMI: 1.45 between 30 and 35, 1.94 between 35 and 40, 2.76 above 40, compared with a BMI of 22.5 to 25, in non-smokers without chronic disease, without accounting for fitness.6 For cardiovascular deaths, the 2025 meta-analysis gives, in fit people, 1.50 for overweight and 1.62 for obesity, with intervals that contain 1: an excess is not demonstrated, but not ruled out either.3

Almost all of these results are observational, from mostly male and American populations, with categories based on BMI, which does not distinguish fat from muscle. No study read sets a personal target.

What this means

Two statements are true at the same time: obesity is an established risk factor, and fitness is an independent lever that you act on more directly than on the scales. One does not contradict the other. What is justified is not making weight your only indicator.

That leaves the practical question: why do so many people not manage to keep going?

The real obstacles, and how to remove them

Knowing what to do is not the bottleneck: the real problem is taking action and sticking with it.

Other people’s gaze and the places

In a survey of 1,397 Chinese students (Li and colleagues, 2025), perceived weight stigma was correlated with avoidance of exercise (r = 0.41), partly through internalised shame and social anxiety; only 1.6% of participants were living with obesity and the study is cross-sectional.27 A British qualitative study (Flint and Reale, 2018, 30 young regular exercisers) reports hostile attitudes towards people with obesity and suggests a perceived barrier to access to exercise venues: small sample, qualitative result.28 These sources are thin. They justify only a practical consequence: choose a setting where you are comfortable (at home, outdoors, a quiet time slot, supportive guidance). That is organisation, not weakness.

Pain, joints, breath

I could not read any source that compares the joint load of walking, cycling or aquatic exercise in people living with obesity, or that quantifies an effect on pain. The sources read cite walking, cycling and swimming as examples, without evaluating their effect on the joint.8 Preferring these activities to running or jumping at the start is therefore a coaching proposal, not demonstrated here. For breathing, the HAS uses an effort scale out of 10: about 5 to 6 for moderate activity, 7 to 8 for sustained activity.18 You should be able to keep going, out of breath but not panicking.

Sticking with it: what research knows about habit

In a study by Lally and colleagues (2010), 96 students repeated a chosen behaviour every day and rated how automatic it became. It took on average 66 days to reach maximum automaticity, but from 18 to about 254 days depending on the person; exercise habits took about 1.5 times longer than drinking or eating habits; and a single missed day changed the result little.24

A habit is built over weeks, with large differences from one person to another

Days needed to reach maximum automaticity, study of 96 students followed for 84 days; the value of 254 days is a modelled estimate beyond the end of the study. Automaticity was self-reported. Source: Lally et al., European Journal of Social Psychology, 2010, read in a British Psychological Society report.24

What this means

If it takes you a while, you are not “bad”: the gap between people is huge and the average is two months. Missing one day destroys nothing; missing many repetitions eventually weighs. The aim is not perfection but regularity over several months.

Two tools have evidence in their favour. “Implementation intentions” (deciding in advance when, where and how, in the form “if this situation arises, then I do this action”) have a medium to high effect on achieving goals in a meta-analysis by Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006, 94 tests, d = 0.65).25 And self-monitoring: in the meta-analysis by Michie and colleagues (2009, 122 evaluations, 44,747 adults), interventions that combined self-monitoring with at least one other control technique were more effective (0.42 versus 0.26).26 This translates simply: set a time and a place (“after my morning coffee, I walk for 10 minutes”), and note what you do.

Do not confuse motivation with a system: motivation comes and goes, a system (when, where, what, noting it down) stays.8

The phased action plan

Proposal This plan is a typical pathway built from the sources above; it has not been tested as it stands in a trial. The starting doses are deliberately low, so that you can sustain them. A health professional can adapt it to you.

Before starting: medical advice

The list of cases is drawn from the American College of Sports Medicine (ACSM, 2015) pre-participation algorithm, as described in two reports read. For someone who does not exercise regularly and has no known cardiovascular, metabolic or kidney disease and no symptoms, medical advice is not needed to start at light to moderate intensity. On the other hand, it is recommended if you have a known disease of this kind (type 1 or 2 diabetes, heart, vascular, cerebrovascular or kidney disease), or the slightest suggestive sign: chest pain or discomfort, unusual breathlessness at rest or on light effort, dizziness or faintness, ankle swelling, palpitations, claudication, a known heart murmur, fatigue or breathlessness unusual for your usual activities.20,21 In these reports, obesity, hypertension and dyslipidaemias are classed as risk factors and not as known disease; the ACSM therefore does not have them trigger prior advice on their own.21

My practical advice, which goes beyond the letter of the algorithm: because this profile often combines several factors (diabetes, hypertension, apnoea, joint pain, recent treatment), see your doctor before starting if any of them applies to you, especially if you have not exercised for a long time. The 2022 HAS recommendations fit within care coordinated by the family doctor, with specialist levels of referral,18 and the HAS has also published a recommendation on prescribing physical activity (July 2022, of which I read only the title).19 For blood pressure, the six-minute walk test treats a resting pressure above 180 over 100 mmHg (or a resting heart rate above 120) as a relative contraindication: in that case, the test is done after medical advice.22

Week 0: your starting measurements

Do these tests under conditions you can reproduce (same place, same time, same shoes). They matter more than the scales.

  • 6-minute walk (endurance). Flat course, 30 metres if possible, distance covered in 6 minutes, at your own pace, with your usual aids. This is a standardised test: stop in case of chest pain, intolerable breathlessness, cramp, unsteadiness, excessive sweating or pallor.22 In a study of 214 Chinese adults living with obesity over the age of 40, the mean distance was 523 m (540 in men, 508 in women), with no universal reference value: do not compare yourself with a number, compare yourself with yourself.23
  • Chair stand (leg strength). Number of times you stand up from a stable chair, arms crossed, in 30 seconds, or time for 5 stands. This is a classic field test; I did not read a norm in people living with obesity, so I do not cite one.
  • A strength test from the site (depending on the page), to keep a record of your progress in strength training.
  • Weight, if you wish. It is optional, never the main criterion. If the number makes you feel bad, you do not have to track it.

Measurement noise is real: the ATS indicates that a second walk test done the next day gives on average 0 to 17% more (learning effect) and that performance stabilises after about two tests in the week.22 In the Chinese study, two successive tests gave 508 and 517 m on average (reliability of 0.89).23 So do a practice run the week before, or keep the better of the two, and do not mistake a variation of a few metres for progress.

The thread of the plan

A gradual build-up, below the HAS target for two months

Proposed progression of moderate-effort activity time (5 to 6 out of 10) over 12 weeks. The 150-minute marker is the lower end of the HAS range (2 h 30 to 3 h per week, reached gradually).18 The steps are a proposal, not derived from a trial.

Weeks 1 to 4: set up the system (60 to 90 minutes per week)

  • Typical sessions. Four to six walks or bike rides of 10 to 15 minutes, at light to moderate effort, at a fixed time. The AHA gives walks of 10 to 20 minutes a day as an example.8 One or two 15-minute strength sessions with your body weight: standing up from a chair, pushing against a wall, stepping up onto a step.
  • System. One “if, then” sentence per session, noted in a notebook or an app. Tick each session done, that is all.
  • Dose. Less than you think you can do. You should finish each session wanting to do it again.
  • Move on when you have kept it up for four weeks without pain that is still there the next day, even with short sessions. Step back or stay when you have skipped more than half the sessions: reduce the dose, not the ambition.

Weeks 5 to 8: build up the duration (90 to 150 minutes per week)

  • Typical sessions. Three to five sessions of 20 to 30 minutes, moderate effort (5 to 6 out of 10, you can talk in short sentences). Two strength sessions of 20 to 25 minutes: chair squat, incline push-ups, band row, supported plank.
  • Progression. Change only one variable at a time (duration, frequency or intensity), in steps of two weeks. One example of a step goal cited by the AHA: from 6,000 to 8,000 steps a day over three months.8
  • Retest, week 6 (optional). Six-minute walk and chair stand, only if you feel well.
  • Move on when the 20 to 30 minutes leave you a little out of breath but not exhausted. Step back when joint pain rises from one session to the next.

Weeks 9 to 12: aim for the target (150 to 180 minutes per week)

  • Typical sessions. Four to five sessions of 30 to 40 minutes of moderate endurance, one of which can become a little more sustained if you tolerate it. Two strength sessions, with a load that becomes demanding in the last 10 to 12 repetitions, which is a practical rule, not a trial result.
  • Target. The HAS recommendations aim for 2 h 30 to 3 h of moderate activity per week, or 1 h 15 to 2 h 30 of vigorous activity, with strength training at least two days a week, and a reduction in sedentary time.18 These values are to be adapted to your abilities.
  • Retest, week 12. Same conditions as in week 0: six-minute walk, chair stand, strength test.

After week 12: maintain and choose

  • Maintenance. Keep the rhythm of the last phase and repeat the tests every three months. For what comes next, the AHA mentions markers of 200 to 300 minutes per week for maintaining lost weight, but that is not your starting goal.8
  • Reading your results. If your walking distance, your number of chair stands or your strength load rise beyond the measurement noise (more than 5 to 10% is a coaching marker, not derived from a study), your fitness is improving, whether the scales move or not.
  • If nothing progresses after three regular months, it is not a failure: talk to a professional (sleep, medications, pain, load, recovery).
What this means

The plan is deliberately slow. The 12 weeks do not make you an athlete: they build the habit and the capacity to tolerate effort. In the research read, the improvement in fitness is measurable, and what matters is regularity over several months.

Common mistakes, warning signs, when to see someone

Common mistakes

  • Starting too hard. First sessions that are too hard end in pain or disgust (coaching experience, no sourced figure).
  • Judging the plan by the scales. Blood pressure, breathing and strength often improve before them, or without them.
  • Forgetting strength. Two sessions a week are enough to start (step 4).
  • Combining exercise with a very restrictive diet without follow-up. The HAS advises against such diets.18
  • Stopping everything after one missed day. One missed day changes the habit little: resume the next day.

Warning signs: stop and see someone

Pain or discomfort in the chest, neck, jaw or arm; unusual breathlessness at rest or on light effort; dizziness or faintness; palpitations; swelling of the ankles; leg pain when walking that forces you to stop. These are the signs the ACSM cites as warranting medical advice.21 For the rest, a practical rule not derived from a trial: sharp joint pain, swelling, or pain that increases the next day justify reducing the dose and asking for advice.

Special cases

Under recent treatment, after bariatric surgery, with diabetes on insulin, untreated apnoea or disabling pain, get support from the person who follows you. For children and teenagers, see P1 and P2.

A straight answer to the question

You asked what movement brings you independently of weight, what you can ask of it for weight, and how to start.

Independently of weight: fitness (measurable), a little less blood pressure and sugar, better nights if you have apnoea, and a health trajectory that, in large cohorts, depends on fitness at every weight. This is solid for the effects measured in trials; it is probable but not demonstrated for survival.

For weight: little on its own. Exercise helps more with maintenance and as a complement to nutritional care, which is a matter for a professional. It also protects muscle.

To start: medical advice if you have a known disease or a symptom, three starting tests, a very low dose, a system (when, where, noting it down), a build-up in steps, retests at 6 and 12 weeks.

Level of certainty. Solid: fitness is associated with health at every weight; exercise lowers blood pressure and blood glucose a little without weight loss; exercise alone brings little weight loss. Probable: strength training protects lean mass during weight loss, including under medication (a hypothesis supported by one trial and the logic of dieting). Untested proposal: the steps of the plan, the choice of walking, cycling or aquatic exercise for the joints, and the progression thresholds.

Limits

What this article does not say
  • This is not personalised medical advice. It does not replace your doctor or the team that follows you.
  • Most of the data are observational and come from mostly male, American and fairly affluent populations.
  • Few exercise trials last more than a year (in the Jayedi meta-analysis, only two trials last more than 48 weeks).
  • I did not read any source comparing the joints under walking, cycling and aquatic exercise, nor any study quantifying the effect on pain; these points are proposals.
  • The effects of strength training under GLP-1 treatment were not specifically tested in the sources read.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to lose weight before I start?

No, according to the sources read: fitness is linked to health at every weight, and exercise works without weight loss. Losing weight remains a subject to discuss with your doctor.

Which activity should I choose?

The one you will do. The sources cite walking, cycling and swimming as examples. No source read ranks these activities for your joints; choose the one that is least painful for you and change if needed.

And if the scales do not move?

That is expected with exercise alone: 150 minutes per week give on average about 2.8 kg less in the 2024 meta-analysis, with large variations. Track your fitness tests.

I am taking a treatment for obesity. Can I do strength training?

Ask the person who follows you. The data read suggest a benefit for lean mass, without a trial dedicated to strength training with these medications.
